standard.title: Diversity and continuity of First Nations Australians
standard.description: the diversity of First Nations Australians, their social organisation and their continuous connection to Country/Place
standard.prior_knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3K04): Students explored the ways First Nations Australians in different parts of Australia are interconnected with Country/Place through poems, songs, paintings and stories.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the diversity of First Nations Australians, their social organisation and their continuous connection to Country/Place.

nodes.label: Diversity within First Nations Australians
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that First Nations Australians include two distinct cultural groups (Aboriginal Peoples and Torres Strait Islander Peoples) and that there is considerable diversity within these groups.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain that Aboriginal Peoples and Torres Strait Islander Peoples are distinct groups and give at least one way they differ.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise the diversity between and within Aboriginal Peoples and Torres Strait Islander Peoples; explore diversity in language, culture, social organisation and connection to Country/Place across different groups.
wider: Research the significant diversity of language groups across Australia and investigate one group in depth
Compare social organisation in two contrasting First Nations Australian groups
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that First Nations Australians are not a single homogeneous group is prerequisite to discussing their social organisation and connection to Country/Place meaningfully.

response_modes.reason: Students often have a unified 'Aboriginal Australians' mental model — explicitly challenge this with evidence of linguistic, cultural and geographic diversity.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The linguistic diversity of First Nations Australians (over 250 language groups) is one of the richest examples of cultural diversity available in the curriculum.
success_criteria: Explains that Aboriginal Peoples and Torres Strait Islander Peoples are distinct groups
Describes at least one way diversity exists within these groups

nodes.label: Continuous connection to Country/Place — archaeological evidence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how archaeological sites show the continuous connection of early First Peoples of Australia to Country/Place.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one archaeological site (e.g. Nauwalabila, Devil's Lair, Lake Mungo) and explain what it shows about continuous connection to Country/Place.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate archaeological sites that show continuous connection of early First Peoples to Country/Place and early lifestyles; explore the connection of First Nations Australians to land and water and how they manage these resources.
wider: Investigate the significance of Lake Mungo specifically and what its evidence tells us about the antiquity of human presence in Australia
Explore how archaeologists work with First Nations communities to investigate these sites respectfully

response_modes.reason: Multiple archaeological sites from different regions demonstrate that continuous connection is not a local phenomenon — breadth strengthens the evidence base.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The archaeological evidence for continuous connection (65,000+ years) is one of the most compelling pieces of historical evidence in the curriculum — exploring multiple sites deepens the concept.
success_criteria: Names at least one archaeological site
Explains what the site reveals about continuous connection to Country/Place

nodes.label: Trade and exchange of ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the diversity and significance of trade and exchange of ideas among First Nations Australians, including with groups outside Australia.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least one example of trade or exchange involving First Nations Australians and explain its significance.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the diversity and significance of trade and exchange of ideas among First Nations Australians, including with groups outside Australia such as the Macassans; connect trade to broader social organisation.
wider: Research the Macassan-First Nations Australian trading relationship in depth and discuss what it reveals about economic and social organisation
Compare First Nations Australian trade networks with those of other cultures in the same historical period

response_modes.reason: Trade and exchange connects social organisation, geographical knowledge and cross-cultural interaction — it integrates multiple aspects of the First Nations Australian descriptor.

success_criteria: Describes at least one example of trade or exchange
Explains the significance of that trade or exchange for First Nations Australian society
